pack.name: Languages
pack.title: The Unspeakable Tongues
pack.blurb: Living and dead languages, scripts, grammar, borrowed words and First Languages.

prompts.text: Name a language that is still spoken today.
prompts.flavor: Some seven thousand tongues still wag in the world above. The deep has been listening to every one.
prompts.rules: Any language with native speakers today, sign languages included, or one revived after dying out, like Hebrew. Dead languages and ones invented for fiction don't count.

answers.lore: The most spoken language on Earth once learners are counted, though Mandarin and Spanish both have more native speakers.
Has more native speakers than any other language: close to a billion.
Really a family of tongues as varied as the Romance languages, held together by one writing system.
Still spoken in Patagonia, by descendants of settlers who sailed to Argentina in 1865.
Ireland's first official language, ranked above English in its constitution.

One of the oldest living languages, with poetry around 2,000 years old.

Jesus spoke it. Its modern forms live on in northern Iraq, a few Syrian villages and the Assyrian diaspora.

Its alphabet has just thirteen letters, one of them the ʻokina, a catch in the throat.

Spoken in the mountain valleys of northern Pakistan, and related to no other known language.
Spoken in Botswana and Namibia, with dozens of click sounds and one of the largest sets of sounds of any language.
Spoken on a tributary of the Amazon. It can be hummed or whistled, and may have no words for exact numbers.

Created by deaf children at new schools in Managua in the 1980s: a rare chance to watch a language being born.
A living language of Quebec and Ontario, not to be confused with the Algonquian family it gave its name to.
Gave English the word kangaroo, noted down by Captain Cook's crew in 1770. Its speakers give directions by compass points, not left and right.
Spoken on North Sentinel Island by a people who refuse all contact, so almost nothing is known of it.
Descended from Doric, the Greek of ancient Sparta, not from the Greek of Athens. A few hundred to a few thousand people, mostly elderly, still speak it.
Spoken by about 2,500 people in one Swedish valley, whose ancestors were still writing in runes in the early 1900s.
Spoken on the island of Bougainville, it has the smallest alphabet in use today: just twelve letters.

prompts.text: Name a dead or extinct language.
prompts.flavor: Words nobody speaks any more, carved into stone and clay. Some of them may still be listening.
prompts.rules: Any language with no native speakers left, ancient or recent. Revived languages count if they died out first, like Cornish.

answers.lore: Dead, though the Vatican still writes in it, and one of its cash machines offered instructions in Latin.
Cracked in 1822 by Champollion, using the Rosetta Stone.
Dolly Pentreath, who died in 1777, is often called its last native speaker. It has since been revived.
Its last native speaker, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974. It has since been revived.

prompts.text: Name a writing system or alphabet.
prompts.flavor: Some marks were made to be read by the living. Others were meant to be read only by the dead.
prompts.rules: Any script, alphabet or other way of writing words, ancient, modern or invented, Braille and shorthand included. Spelling alphabets like NATO's, codes and ciphers don't count.

answers.lore: Named after Saint Cyril, though the alphabet he devised was the older Glagolitic.
The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved on the temple of Philae in AD 394.
Louis Braille, blinded as a small boy, worked it out at fifteen from a military code called night writing.
Legend says Odin hung on a windswept tree for nine nights to win the secret of the runes.
Notches cut along the edge of a standing stone, usually read from the bottom upwards.
Pressed into wet clay with a cut reed, and used for more than 3,000 years.

Deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, an architect, who showed it recorded an early form of Greek.
Its signs can be roughly sounded out using Linear B, but the Minoan language behind them remains unknown.

Nazi Germany promoted it as truly German, then banned it in 1941, falsely calling it Jewish.
Created in 1959 by Shong Lue Yang, a farmer who could not read. His followers call him the Mother of Writing.

Made for the Commander Keen games in 1990. Minecraft players know it from the enchanting table.

The language of angels, according to John Dee and Edward Kelley, who said spirits revealed it to them in the 1580s.

prompts.flavor: Some tongues were invented to unite the world. Others were invented to summon something into it.
prompts.rules: Any language made up on purpose: for the world, for fiction or as an experiment. Language games like Pig Latin, programming languages and codes don't count.

answers.lore: Published in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, an eye doctor in Warsaw, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Built by Marc Okrand for Star Trek III in 1984. Hamlet has been translated into it.
Created by the linguist David J. Peterson for Game of Thrones, with thousands of words.

Orwell's language for 1984, designed to make rebellious thoughts impossible to put into words.

Devised by the abbess Hildegard of Bingen in the 1100s, with about a thousand words and its own letters. Why is a mystery.
Sung by the French band Magma since 1969, invented by their drummer, Christian Vander, for a far-off planet.

prompts.flavor: Speak plainly and the deep ignores you. Speak in figures, and something may answer.
prompts.rules: Any named rhetorical device or trope, like a metaphor or simile. Name the device, not an example of it: 'raining cats and dogs' won't do.

answers.lore: Aristotle thought a gift for metaphor was the one thing a poet could never learn from anyone else.
The word is one itself: Greek for 'sharp-dull'.
Named by John Ruskin in 1856, scornful of poets who make nature share human feelings.

prompts.flavor: Every sentence must end somewhere. Most end in a full stop. Some end in a scream.
prompts.rules: Any mark that punctuates writing, from everyday ones to typographic marks like the asterisk or hash, and rare or proposed ones too. Accents, currency signs and maths symbols don't count.

answers.lore: No one knows where it came from. One tale says scribes shortened Latin quaestio to a Q perched over an o.
Many typewriters had no key for it. Typists struck a full stop, backspaced and typed an apostrophe over it.
The Apostrophe Protection Society closed in 2019. Its founder, then 95, said ignorance and laziness had won.

Italians call it the snail, Danes the elephant's trunk, and the Dutch the little monkey's tail.

A back-to-front question mark proposed by the French poet Alcanter de Brahm in 1899.

Shorthand for 'and' from ancient Rome. It survives on Irish road signs, standing for agus.

A full stop followed by a tilde, proposed in 2007 to show that a remark means more than it says.
؟, turned to face the other way, as Arabic is written from right to left.
A little pointing hand, ☞, drawn in the margins of medieval and Renaissance books to say: look here.
A reversed question mark for rhetorical questions, proposed by the printer Henry Denham in the 1580s. It didn't catch on.

prompts.text: Name a Latin phrase used in English.
prompts.flavor: Latin died long ago, yet still it walks among you, muttering in courtrooms and on tombstones.
prompts.rules: A phrase of two or more Latin words, or the Latin behind an abbreviation like etc. or e.g. Single words like ergo or alibi don't count.

aliases: Carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero
answers.lore: From Horace, who added that you should trust as little as possible to tomorrow.
Caesar's report to Rome of a lightning victory in 47 BC.
